title: Τηλέμαχος ἐν Πύλῳ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: At sunrise Telemachus and Athena, still in the likeness of Mentor, reach Pylos, where the people are sacrificing black bulls to Poseidon on the shore. Athena tells the young man to put his shame aside and go straight to Nestor. Nestor's son Peisistratus welcomes the strangers to the feast and hands the cup first to the older guest, and Athena prays to Poseidon for Nestor, for the Pylians and for the success of the voyage. When the meal is over Nestor asks who they are, and Telemachus, given courage by Athena, says that they come from Ithaca and begs for any true word of his father's fate.

sentences.t:
Ἠέλιος δ’ ἀνόρουσε, λιπὼν περικαλλέα λίμνην,
οὐρανὸν ἐς πολύχαλκον, ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι φαείνοι
καὶ θνητοῖσι βροτοῖσιν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν·
sentences.tr:
Ēelios d’ anorouse, lipōn perikallea limnēn,
ouranon es polychalkon, hin’ athanatoisi phaeinoi
kai thnētoisi brotoisin epi zeidōron arouran·
sentences.i: The Sun sprang up, leaving the very beautiful mere, into the sky of much bronze, to shine for the immortals and for mortal men upon the grain-giving plough-land;
sentences.n: Ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος 'sun', here the Sun as a god. ἀνόρουσε, aorist of ἀνορούω 'spring up', has no augment: Homer's past tenses may drop it, and the augmented form would be ἀνώρουσε. The λίμνη he leaves is the stream of Ocean, pictured as a mere at the edge of the world. πολύχαλκος 'rich in bronze' pictures the sky as a vault of metal. ἵνα with the optative φαείνοι, after a past verb, gives the purpose. ζείδωρος is usually explained as 'giving ζειά', a kind of grain, so 'grain-giving'; an ancient alternative made it 'life-giving', from ζάω. ἄρουρα is tilled land. The δ’ joins this book to what went before.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ Πύλον, Νηλῆος ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
ἷξον·
sentences.tr:
hoi de Pylon, Nēlēos eyktimenon ptoliethron,
hixon·
sentences.l:
and they to Pylos, Neleus' well-built citadel,
came;
sentences.i: and they came to Pylos, the well-built citadel of Neleus;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is 'and they', Telemachus and his crew: what looks like the article is in Homer a pronoun, and this pattern recurs constantly. ἷξον is the aorist of ἵκω 'come, arrive', and takes the place reached in the accusative without a preposition, as poetry allows. Whether it is augmented cannot be seen, since an augment would only lengthen an ι that is long already. Νηλῆος is the epic genitive of Νηλεύς (Attic -έως); Neleus is Nestor's father. ἐυκτίμενος 'well-built' joins ἐυ- 'well' to a participle of κτίζω 'found, build'. πτολίεθρον 'citadel' is an epic derivative of πτόλις. The verb is held back to the head of line 5.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ θινὶ θαλάσσης ἱερὰ ῥέζον,
ταύρους παμμέλανας, ἐνοσίχθονι κυανοχαίτῃ.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ epi thini thalassēs hiera rhezon,
taurous pammelanas, enosichthoni kyanochaitēi.
sentences.l:
and they, upon the shore of the sea, were performing sacred-rites,
bulls all-black, to the dark-haired earth-shaker.
sentences.i: The people there were offering sacrifice on the shore of the sea, bulls all black, to the dark-haired earth-shaker.
sentences.n: τοί is another pronoun-form of the article, 'they', and marks a change of subject: the men of Pylos, not the travellers. ῥέζον is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔρρεζον), and ἱερὰ ῥέζειν, 'do sacred things', is the regular phrase for offering sacrifice; ταύρους stands in apposition to ἱερά and names the victims. παμμέλας is 'all-black'; dark victims suit gods of the sea and of the world below. ἐνοσίχθων is Poseidon's epithet 'earth-shaker'. κυανοχαίτης joins κύανος, a dark blue-black substance, to χαίτη 'flowing hair': 'dark-haired'.

sentences.t:
ἐννέα δ’ ἕδραι ἔσαν, πεντακόσιοι δ’ ἐν ἑκάστῃ
ἥατο καὶ προύχοντο ἑκάστοθι ἐννέα ταύρους.
sentences.tr:
ennea d’ hedrai esan, pentakosioi d’ en hekastēi
hēato kai prouchonto hekastothi ennea taurous.
sentences.l:
Nine were the companies, and five hundred in each
were sitting, and they held before them in each place nine bulls.
sentences.i: There were nine companies, with five hundred men sitting in each, and each company had nine bulls set before it.
sentences.n: ἕδρα is a seat, here a row of seats and so a company seated together. Nine companies of five hundred make four thousand five hundred men, and nine bulls apiece make eighty-one. ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν. ἥατο is the epic third plural of ἧστο 'were sitting' (Attic ἧντο), with the Ionic ending -ατο for -ντο. προύχοντο is a contracted compound of πρό and ἔχω, middle: 'held before them, had ready'. ἑκάστοθι has the suffix -θι of place where, 'in each place'; the suffixes -θι, -θεν and -δε mark place where, place from and place to.

sentences.t:
εὖθ’ οἱ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο, θεῷ δ’ ἐπὶ μηρί’ ἔκαιον,
οἱ δ’ ἰθὺς κατάγοντο ἰδ’ ἱστία νηὸς ἐίσης
στεῖλαν ἀείραντες, τὴν δ’ ὥρμισαν, ἐκ δ’ ἔβαν αὐτοί·
sentences.tr:
euth’ hoi splanchna pasanto, theōi d’ epi mēri’ ekaion,
hoi d’ ithys katagonto id’ histia nēos eisēs
steilan aeirantes, tēn d’ hōrmisan, ek d’ eban autoi·
sentences.i: When the Pylians had tasted the entrails and were burning the thigh-pieces for the god, the travellers put straight in to shore, hauled up and furled the sails of their well-balanced ship, moored her, and stepped out themselves;
sentences.n: εὖτε is 'when'. οἱ and οἱ δέ are pronouns for two groups, the Pylians at their sacrifice and the crew coming in. πάσαντο, aorist middle of πατέομαι 'taste', is unaugmented; the σπλάγχνα, heart, liver and other innards, were roasted and tasted first. μηρί’ is μηρία, the thigh-pieces burned for the god; ἔκαιον keeps its augment. κατάγοντο 'put in to land' is unaugmented (Attic κατήγοντο), and so is στεῖλαν 'furled' (Attic ἔστειλαν), while ὥρμισαν, with ὀ- lengthened to ὠ-, and ἔβαν (= ἔβησαν) keep theirs. ἰδέ is an epic 'and'. ἐίσης, of a ship, is usually taken as 'well-balanced', equal on both sides; the sense is not certain.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος νηὸς βαῖν’, ἦρχε δ’ Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: ek d’ ara Tēlemachos nēos bain’, ērche d’ Athēnē.
sentences.l: And then Telemachus went out of the ship, and Athena led the way.
sentences.i: Then Telemachus climbed out of the ship, with Athena going first.
sentences.n: The line reverses the first line of the embarkation at 2.416, with ἐκ 'out of' in place of ἀν(ά) 'up on to', and the same English is kept for what is the same. ἐκ … βαῖν’ is tmesis of ἐκβαίνω 'go out', with νηός the genitive 'out of the ship'. βαῖν’ is βαῖνε, an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔβαινε). ἦρχε, from ἄρχω, keeps its augment (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-) and here means 'went first, led the way'. ἄρα is a light 'then', marking the next step in the story. Athena is still in the likeness of Mentor, as Telemachus's words at line 22 show.

sentences.t: τὸν προτέρη προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton proterē proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him first addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: The goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, was the first to speak to him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction on the pattern of τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε, with προτέρη 'first, before him' in place of δ’ αὖτε 'in turn': no one has spoken yet, and she speaks before he does. προτέρη agrees with θεά and shows Ionic η. τόν is the pronoun 'him'. προσέειπε is προσεῖπε with its augment left uncontracted before the root's own ει-; it is an augmented form. The line ends with a raised point, and the speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχ’, οὐ μέν σε χρὴ ἔτ’ αἰδοῦς, οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν·
sentences.tr: Tēlemach’, ou men se chrē et’ aidous, oud’ ēbaion·
sentences.l: “Telemachus, there is no need for you any longer of shame, not even a little;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you have no need of shame any longer, not the least bit;
sentences.n: Τηλέμαχ’ is the vocative Τηλέμαχε, elided. χρή with the accusative σε and the genitive αἰδοῦς is 'there is need for you of'. μέν is here the emphatic particle, a weaker μήν. αἰδώς is the shame, reserve or respect that holds a person back in front of others, and the exchange turns on it: Telemachus names it again at line 24. ἠβαιόν 'a little' is almost always found with a negative, as in οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν 'not even a little'. ἔτ’ is ἔτι: the time for holding back is over.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα γὰρ καὶ πόντον ἐπέπλως, ὄφρα πύθηαι
πατρός, ὅπου κύθε γαῖα καὶ ὅν τινα πότμον ἐπέσπεν.
sentences.tr:
touneka gar kai ponton epeplōs, ophra pythēai
patros, hopou kythe gaia kai hon tina potmon epespen.
sentences.l:
for this reason indeed you have sailed over the open-sea, so that you may learn
of your father, where the earth covered him and what fate he met.
sentences.i: for this is the very reason you have sailed across the sea, to learn of your father, where the earth has hidden him and what fate he met.
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is crasis of τοῦ ἕνεκα, 'for this reason', and points forward to the purpose clause with ὄφρα 'so that'. ἐπέπλως is an old root aorist of ἐπιπλέω, 'sail over', with πόντον as its object (Attic ἐπέπλευσας). πύθηαι is the aorist subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι with the ending left uncontracted (Attic πύθῃ). κύθε is the unaugmented aorist of κεύθω 'cover, hide': the words allow that he is dead and buried. ὅν τινα, printed as two words, is the indirect interrogative ὅστις, 'what', agreeing with πότμον; this ὅν is not the possessive 'his own'. πότμον ἐπισπεῖν, from ἐφέπω, is 'meet one's fate', used of death.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἰθὺς κίε Νέστορος ἱπποδάμοιο·
sentences.tr: all’ age nyn ithys kie Nestoros hippodamoio·
sentences.l: But come now, go straight for horse-taming Nestor;
sentences.i: But come now, go straight to Nestor, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: ἄγε is an imperative used as an interjection, 'come'. κίε is the imperative of κίω 'go', and ἰθύς 'straight' takes the genitive of the person made for: 'straight for Nestor'. ἱπποδάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). ἱππόδαμος 'horse-taming' is a standing epithet, translated the same way each time it comes. Nestor is the old king of Pylos, whom Athena told Telemachus in Book 1 to question first.

sentences.t: εἴδομεν ἥν τινα μῆτιν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κέκευθε.
sentences.tr: eidomen hēn tina mētin eni stēthessi kekeuthe.
sentences.l: let us find out what counsel in his breast he keeps hidden.
sentences.i: let us find out what counsel he keeps hidden in his breast.
sentences.n: εἴδομεν looks like an indicative, but is the subjunctive of οἶδα 'know', from the stem εἰδ-, with a short vowel (Attic εἰδῶμεν), used as an exhortation: 'let us know, let us find out'. Short-vowel subjunctives of this kind are common in Homer. ἥν τινα is the indirect interrogative again, like ὅν τινα in line 16. μῆτις is practical intelligence, a plan or counsel. κέκευθε is the perfect of κεύθω, the verb of κύθε in line 16, with present sense, 'holds hidden'. ἐνί is ἐν, and στήθεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι: the breast is the seat of thought.

sentences.t: λίσσεσθαι δέ μιν αὐτός, ὅπως νημερτέα εἴπῃ·
sentences.tr: lissesthai de min autos, hopōs nēmertea eipēi·
sentences.l: And beseech him yourself, so that he may speak unerring things;
sentences.i: And entreat him yourself to tell you what is unerring;
sentences.n: λίσσεσθαι is an infinitive used as an imperative, a common Homeric turn: 'beseech'. αὐτός, nominative, is 'you yourself', agreeing with the unexpressed subject. μιν is the epic accusative pronoun 'him' (Attic αὐτόν) and is very common. ὅπως with the subjunctive εἴπῃ gives the purpose. νημερτέα is the uncontracted neuter plural of νημερτής 'unerring', from νη- 'not' and the root of ἁμαρτάνω 'miss the mark': words that do not miss the truth.

sentences.t: ψεῦδος δ’ οὐκ ἐρέει·
sentences.tr: pseudos d’ ouk ereei·
sentences.l: and a falsehood he will not speak;
sentences.i: he will not tell a falsehood;
sentences.n: ἐρέει is the uncontracted future of the stem ἐρ- 'say' (Attic ἐρεῖ). Homer leaves many such vowels open that Attic contracts, and ἐξερέεσθαι at line 24 is another. ψεῦδος 'a falsehood' stands first for emphasis. The short clause, closed by a raised point, is Athena's assurance before she gives its reason.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ πεπνυμένος ἐστί.
sentences.tr: mala gar pepnymenos esti.
sentences.l: for he is very prudent.”
sentences.i: for he is very prudent.”
sentences.n: πεπνυμένος is a perfect participle belonging to πνέω, 'having breath, having spirit', and so 'sensible, prudent'. It is the standing epithet of Telemachus, rendered 'prudent' every time, and here it is said of Nestor as a plain predicate; the English keeps the same word so that the link is heard. ἐστί closes the line and Athena's first speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The whole line is a reply-formula used unchanged wherever Telemachus answers face to face, and it takes the same English every time. τήν is the pronoun 'her'. αὖ is 'in turn'. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak', augmented (αὐ- lengthened to ηὐ-), and ἀντίον 'face to face, in reply' is an adverb. He speaks to Athena as Mentor, whose shape she wears.

sentences.t: Μέντορ, πῶς τ’ ἄρ’ ἴω;
sentences.tr: Mentor, pōs t’ ar’ iō;
sentences.l: “Mentor, how then am I to go?
sentences.i: “Mentor, how am I to go?
sentences.n: Μέντορ is the vocative of Μέντωρ: Athena has the form of Mentor, the old companion of Odysseus in Ithaca. ἴω is the subjunctive of εἶμι 'go', used in a question of doubt: 'how am I to go?'. τ’ is τε and ἄρ’ is ἄρα; together they give the question a note of bewilderment that has no word-for-word English equivalent. The edition prints a question mark in mid-line, and a second question follows at once.

sentences.t: πῶς τ’ ἂρ προσπτύξομαι αὐτόν;
sentences.tr: pōs t’ ar prosptyxomai auton;
sentences.l: And how then shall I greet him?
sentences.i: How shall I greet him?
sentences.n: The second question repeats the first up to the verb. ἂρ is the shortened form of ἄρα before a consonant; in the first question it stood elided, ἄρ’. προσπτύξομαι is from προσπτύσσομαι, literally 'fold oneself to', and so 'greet, embrace', or 'address warmly'. It may be a future or, like ἴω, an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel (= προσπτύξωμαι); the sense is much the same. αὐτόν is Nestor.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί πω μύθοισι πεπείρημαι πυκινοῖσιν·
sentences.tr: oude ti pō mythoisi pepeirēmai pykinoisin·
sentences.l: Nor at all am I yet practised in speeches, shrewd ones;
sentences.i: I have no practice yet in shrewd speaking;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι πω is 'not at all as yet'. πεπείρημαι is the perfect of πειράομαι 'try, test', with Ionic η for Attic long α: 'I have made trial of, have experience in', with the dative μύθοισι. μῦθος in Homer is a speech or a thing said. πυκινός means 'close, compact', and of words and thoughts 'shrewd, well-knit'; it stands apart from its noun, at the end of the line. What Telemachus pleads is his youth, as the next line makes plain.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς δ’ αὖ νέον ἄνδρα γεραίτερον ἐξερέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: aidōs d’ au neon andra geraiteron exereesthai.
sentences.l: and again, shame it is for a young man an older one to question.”
sentences.i: and besides, it is a thing of shame for a young man to question an older one.”
sentences.n: αἰδώς takes up the word Athena used in line 14: she told him that he had no more need of shame, and he answers that shame is exactly what a young man feels. The sentence has no verb, and ἐστί is to be understood. νέον ἄνδρα is the subject of the infinitive ἐξερέεσθαι 'question, inquire of', the uncontracted present infinitive of ἐξερέομαι, an epic by-form of ἐξέρομαι, and γεραίτερον, the comparative of γεραιός 'old', is its object. αὖ is 'on the other hand, besides'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The line is a fixed reply-formula, τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε, and answers the variant with προτέρη at line 13 that began Athena's first speech: then she spoke first, now she speaks in turn. αὖτε is 'in turn'. θεά and γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη stand in apposition. γλαυκῶπις joins γλαυκός 'gleaming' to ὤψ 'eye, face'; the exact sense is uncertain, and it is rendered 'gleaming-eyed' every time.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἄλλα μὲν αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ σῇσι νοήσεις,
ἄλλα δὲ καὶ δαίμων ὑποθήσεται·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, alla men autos eni phresi sēisi noēseis,
alla de kai daimōn hypothēsetai·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, some things you yourself in your own mind will think of,
and others a divinity too will prompt;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, some things you will think of for yourself in your own mind, and others a divinity will prompt you with;
sentences.n: ἄλλα μέν … ἄλλα δέ is 'some things … others'. σῇσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι of σός 'your'; the long dative endings -ῃσι, -οισι, -εσσι are everywhere in Homer. φρεσί is the dative of φρένες, the seat of thought. δαίμων is a divine power left unnamed, 'some god'; the speaker is herself a goddess in disguise, which gives the word its edge here. ὑποθήσεται is the future middle of ὑποτίθημι 'put under', and so 'suggest, advise'. νοήσεις 'you will think of' is the human half of the pair.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀίω
οὔ σε θεῶν ἀέκητι γενέσθαι τε τραφέμεν τε.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oiō
ou se theōn aekēti genesthai te traphemen te.
sentences.l:
for I do not think
that you, against the will of the gods, were born and reared.”
sentences.i: for I do not think that you were born and brought up against the will of the gods.”
sentences.n: ὀίω 'I think' is an epic form of οἴομαι. The second οὔ repeats the first and does not cancel it: Greek piles up negatives for emphasis. ἀέκητι with the genitive is 'against the will of', and the sense is that the gods have favoured him from birth. γενέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of γίγνομαι, and τραφέμεν an epic infinitive in -έμεν of the intransitive aorist of τρέφω, 'to grow up, be reared'. τε … τε joins the two: born and brought up alike.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ ἡγήσατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
καρπαλίμως·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas’ hēgēsato Pallas Athēnē
karpalimōs·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, Pallas Athena led the way,
swiftly;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Pallas Athena led the way swiftly;
sentences.n: The unit repeats a verse and a word from 2.405 and keeps its English. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’, 'so then having spoken', closes a speech with a participle; φωνήσασ’ is φωνήσασα, elided. ἡγήσατο, aorist of ἡγέομαι 'lead the way', cannot show an augment, since its initial ἡ- is long already. Παλλάς is a title of Athena of uncertain origin; the ancients connected it with πάλλω 'brandish'. καρπαλίμως 'swiftly' runs over into the next line.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα μετ’ ἴχνια βαῖνε θεοῖο.
sentences.tr: ho d’ epeita met’ ichnia baine theoio.
sentences.l: And he then walked following in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.i: and he followed close behind in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.n: The whole line stands already at 2.406 and keeps the English it has there. ὁ δ’ is the pronoun, 'and he', Telemachus. βαῖνε is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔβαινε). μετ’ may go with ἴχνια, 'after the tracks', or with βαῖνε as tmesis for μετέβαινε, 'walked after'; either way he follows close behind. θεοῖο is a genitive in -οιο of θεός, a noun that Homer uses of a goddess as well as of a god, so the English 'god' does not mean that she is taken for a man. The narrator names her divine, though to Telemachus she is still Mentor.

sentences.t:
ἷξον δ’ ἐς Πυλίων ἀνδρῶν ἄγυρίν τε καὶ ἕδρας,
ἔνθ’ ἄρα Νέστωρ ἧστο σὺν υἱάσιν, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
δαῖτ’ ἐντυνόμενοι κρέα τ’ ὤπτων ἄλλα τ’ ἔπειρον.
sentences.tr:
hixon d’ es Pyliōn andrōn agyrin te kai hedras,
enth’ ara Nestōr hēsto syn huiasin, amphi d’ hetairoi
dait’ entynomenoi krea t’ ōptōn alla t’ epeiron.
sentences.l:
And they came to the gathering and the seats of the Pylian men,
where then Nestor was sitting with his sons, and around, his companions,
preparing the feast, were roasting meat and piercing other pieces on spits.
sentences.i: They came to the gathering and the seats of the men of Pylos, where Nestor was sitting with his sons, while around them his companions were making the feast ready, roasting some of the meat and spitting the rest.
sentences.n: ἷξον is the verb of line 5, now with ἐς. ἄγυρις is an old form of ἀγορά, 'gathering'. ἧστο 'was sitting' is the past of ἧμαι. υἱάσιν is an epic dative plural of υἱός, from a stem υἱ-. δαῖτ’ ἐντυνόμενοι, 'making ready the feast', says what the companions are doing, and ὤπτων and ἔπειρον say how: roasting and piercing with spits. ὤπτων (ὀ- lengthened to ὠ-) and ἔπειρον both keep their augments. κρέα τ’ … ἄλλα τ’ is 'the meat … and other pieces': one lot is on the fire while more is being spitted.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὡς οὖν ξείνους ἴδον, ἁθρόοι ἦλθον ἅπαντες,
χερσίν τ’ ἠσπάζοντο καὶ ἑδριάασθαι ἄνωγον.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hōs oun xeinous idon, hathrooi ēlthon hapantes,
chersin t’ ēspazonto kai hedriaasthai anōgon.
sentences.l:
And they, when they saw the strangers, in a body came, all of them,
and with their hands were greeting them and bade them be seated.
sentences.i: When they saw the strangers, they all came crowding up together, clasped them by the hand in welcome, and bade them sit down.
sentences.n: ὡς οὖν is 'when, then' in narrative. ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist (Attic εἶδον), while ἦλθον and ἠσπάζοντο (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-) keep their augments. ξεῖνος is the epic spelling of ξένος, and the word is both 'stranger' and 'guest': the strangers are received as guests before anyone asks who they are. ἑδριάασθαι is ἑδριᾶσθαι, 'to seat themselves', with the contracted vowel stretched back out to fit the verse; this artificial stretching is called diectasis. ἄνωγον is an unaugmented past form (augmented ἤνωγον) of ἄνωγα 'command', a perfect with present sense.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
ἀμφοτέρων ἕλε χεῖρα καὶ ἵδρυσεν παρὰ δαιτὶ
κώεσιν ἐν μαλακοῖσιν ἐπὶ ψαμάθοις ἁλίῃσιν
πάρ τε κασιγνήτῳ Θρασυμήδεϊ καὶ πατέρι ᾧ·
sentences.tr:
prōtos Nestoridēs Peisistratos engythen elthōn
amphoterōn hele cheira kai hidrysen para daiti
kōesin en malakoisin epi psamathois haliēisin
par te kasignētōi Thrasymēdeï kai pateri hōi·
sentences.l:
First Nestor's son Peisistratus, coming near,
of both took the hand and seated them by the feast
on soft fleeces upon the sands of the sea,
beside his brother Thrasymedes and his own father;
sentences.i: First of all Nestor's son Peisistratus came up close, took each of them by the hand, and seated them at the feast on soft fleeces laid on the sea-sands, beside his brother Thrasymedes and his own father;
sentences.n: Νεστορίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Nestor', set before the personal name. ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω (Attic εἷλε). ἵδρυσεν, from ἱδρύω 'seat', cannot show an augment, since its ι would only be lengthened. κώεσιν is a dative plural of κῶας 'fleece', laid on the sand as seats. ἁλίῃσιν, from ἅλς 'sea', is a dative in -ῃσι: 'sands of the sea'. πάρ is παρά shortened. ᾧ is the possessive ὅς, 'his own father', easily taken for the relative 'to whom'. The guests are given the place of honour beside the king.

sentences.t:
δῶκε δ’ ἄρα σπλάγχνων μοίρας, ἐν δ’ οἶνον ἔχευεν
χρυσείῳ δέπαϊ·
sentences.tr:
dōke d’ ara splanchnōn moiras, en d’ oinon echeuen
chryseiōi depaï·
sentences.l:
And he gave them then portions of the entrails, and poured in wine
in a golden cup;
sentences.i: Then he gave them portions of the entrails and poured wine into a golden cup;
sentences.n: δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (Attic ἔδωκε). σπλάγχνων is a partitive genitive with μοίρας 'shares': the guests get their part of the innards tasted at line 9. ἐν … ἔχευεν is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb, for ἐνέχευεν 'poured in'; ἔχευεν keeps its augment. χρυσείῳ is the epic form of Attic χρυσῷ 'golden', uncontracted. δέπαϊ is the dative of δέπας 'cup', with its ending sounded as a separate syllable.

sentences.t:
δειδισκόμενος δὲ προσηύδα
Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην κούρην Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.tr:
deidiskomenos de prosēuda
Pallad’ Athēnaiēn kourēn Dios aigiochoio·
sentences.l:
and, pledging her, he spoke
to Pallas Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus:
sentences.i: and, pledging her with the cup, he spoke to Pallas Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus:
sentences.n: δειδισκόμενος, from δειδίσκομαι 'greet, pledge', is the gesture of holding out the cup in welcome. προσηύδα 'spoke to' takes the accusative of the person addressed and keeps its augment (αὐ- to ηὐ-). Ἀθηναίη is a longer form of Ἀθήνη. αἰγιόχοιο is a genitive in -οιο of αἰγίοχος, a title of Zeus whose meaning is disputed: usually 'holding the aegis', the goatskin (αἴξ 'goat') shield or cape that terrifies enemies, though other derivations were proposed in antiquity. The whole line names Athena by title and parentage; Peisistratus himself sees only an older man.

sentences.t: εὔχεο νῦν, ὦ ξεῖνε, Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr: eucheo nyn, ō xeine, Poseidaōni anakti·
sentences.l: “Pray now, O stranger, to Poseidon the lord;
sentences.i: “Pray now, stranger, to lord Poseidon;
sentences.n: εὔχεο is the present imperative of εὔχομαι with its vowels left open (Attic εὔχου). ὦ ξεῖνε is a courteous address, 'stranger': the host does not yet know the guests' names and will not ask before the meal. ἄναξ 'lord' is the old word for a king or master, used of gods and of men. Ποσειδάωνι is the uncontracted form of the name, Attic Ποσειδῶνι. The phrase Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι closes the line and closes line 54 again.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ καὶ δαίτης ἠντήσατε δεῦρο μολόντες.
sentences.tr: tou gar kai daitēs ēntēsate deuro molontes.
sentences.l: for it is his feast, too, that you have met with, coming here.
sentences.i: for it is his feast that you have come upon in coming here.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun, a genitive 'his', depending on δαίτης. ἠντήσατε, aorist of ἀντάω 'meet with', takes the genitive and keeps its augment (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-). μολόντες is the aorist participle of βλώσκω 'come, go', a verb whose aorist ἔμολον is poetic. The sacrifice is Poseidon's, so the newcomers, arriving in the middle of it, have become sharers in the god's feast, and courtesy asks them to pray first.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν σπείσῃς τε καὶ εὔξεαι, ἣ θέμις ἐστί,
δὸς καὶ τούτῳ ἔπειτα δέπας μελιηδέος οἴνου
σπεῖσαι, ἐπεὶ καὶ τοῦτον ὀίομαι ἀθανάτοισιν
εὔχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn speisēis te kai euxeai, hē themis esti,
dos kai toutōi epeita depas meliēdeos oinou
speisai, epei kai touton oiomai athanatoisin
euchesthai·
sentences.l:
But when you have poured and prayed, as is right,
give to this man also then the cup of honey-sweet wine
to pour, since this man too, I think, to the immortals
prays;
sentences.i: And when you have poured your libation and prayed, as is right, then give this man too the cup of honey-sweet wine to pour from, since I think that he too prays to the immortals;
sentences.n: ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν, 'when', with the subjunctives σπείσῃς and εὔξεαι. εὔξεαι is an aorist subjunctive with a short vowel and its ending left open (Attic εὔξῃ). σπένδω is to pour a libation, a little wine poured out for the god before drinking. In ἣ θέμις ἐστί, 'as is right', ἥ is the relative pronoun, feminine by attraction to θέμις, 'which is right'; θέμις is established custom. μελιηδής is 'honey-sweet'. τούτῳ and τοῦτον point to the second guest. The infinitive εὔχεσθαι runs over into line 48.

sentences.t: πάντες δὲ θεῶν χατέουσ’ ἄνθρωποι.
sentences.tr: pantes de theōn chateous’ anthrōpoi.
sentences.l: and all men have need of the gods.
sentences.i: and all men stand in need of the gods.
sentences.n: χατέουσ’ is χατέουσι, uncontracted (Attic χατοῦσι), from χατέω 'need, lack', with the genitive θεῶν. The half-line is a general truth, given as a maxim: πάντες and ἄνθρωποι frame the clause, first word and last. It is the reason why the older guest too will wish to pray, and it is spoken with courtesy and piety at once.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ νεώτερός ἐστιν, ὁμηλικίη δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ·
sentences.tr: alla neōteros estin, homēlikiē d’ emoi autōi·
sentences.l: But he is younger, of one age with me myself;
sentences.i: But he is the younger, the same age as I am myself;
sentences.n: νεώτερος 'younger' is said of Telemachus, compared with his companion. ὁμηλικίη is a noun, 'people of the same age', used here as a predicate of one person: 'he is my age-mate'. It has Ionic η for Attic long α. ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ is 'me myself'. The reason for handing the cup first to the other guest is age: honour goes to the elder, the point Telemachus himself made at line 24.

sentences.t: τοὔνεκα σοὶ προτέρῳ δώσω χρύσειον ἄλεισον.
sentences.tr: touneka soi proterōi dōsō chryseion aleison.
sentences.l: therefore to you first I shall give the golden goblet.”
sentences.i: so it is to you that I shall give the golden goblet first.”
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα again, here 'therefore', looking back to the reason just given. προτέρῳ 'first, before him' agrees with σοί. χρύσειον 'golden' has the uncontracted ending -ειος, like χρυσείῳ at line 41. ἄλεισον 'goblet' is a second word for the δέπας of line 41, and the narrative uses both of the one cup. The future δώσω speaks of what he is doing as he speaks. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χειρὶ τίθει δέπας ἡδέος οἴνου·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn en cheiri tithei depas hēdeos oinou·
sentences.l: So having spoken, in her hand he placed the cup of sweet wine;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and put the cup of sweet wine into her hand;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών, 'so having spoken', closes the speech with a participle, and the action follows at once. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι (Attic ἐτίθει). ἡδέος is the genitive of ἡδύς 'sweet', the same in Attic; it stands here where μελιηδέος stood in line 46. ἐν χειρί is 'in the hand': the English must choose a pronoun, and 'her' follows the narrator, who speaks of the goddess, not of the disguise.

sentences.t:
χαῖρε δ’ Ἀθηναίη πεπνυμένῳ ἀνδρὶ δικαίῳ,
οὕνεκα οἷ προτέρῃ δῶκε χρύσειον ἄλεισον·
sentences.tr:
chaire d’ Athēnaiē pepnymenōi andri dikaiōi,
houneka hoi proterēi dōke chryseion aleison·
sentences.l:
And Athena rejoiced in the prudent man, the just one,
because to her first he had given the golden goblet;
sentences.i: And Athena was glad of the prudent and just young man, because he had given the golden goblet to her first;
sentences.n: χαῖρε is an unaugmented imperfect of χαίρω, 'was glad', with the dative of the cause, πεπνυμένῳ ἀνδρὶ δικαίῳ. πεπνυμένος is the house 'prudent', here given to Peisistratus. δίκαιος 'just' is one who gives what is due, here the order of courtesy between older and younger. οὕνεκα is οὗ ἕνεκα, 'because'. οἷ, accented, is the dative pronoun 'to her'. προτέρῃ is feminine, agreeing with οἷ: the narrator again speaks of the goddess, although the youth thinks he is honouring an older man.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ εὔχετο πολλὰ Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι·
sentences.tr: autika d’ eucheto polla Poseidaōni anakti·
sentences.l: and at once she prayed much to Poseidon the lord:
sentences.i: and at once she prayed earnestly to lord Poseidon:
sentences.n: εὔχετο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι 'pray'; with verbs in εὐ- a lengthening to ηὐ- is often not written, so no augment can be read from the form. πολλά is adverbial, 'much, earnestly'. The line closes with Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι, the phrase that closed line 43: she does exactly what she was asked. The goddess prays to Poseidon, her father's brother, for success in an errand that she herself is guiding.

sentences.t:
κλῦθι, Ποσείδαον γαιήοχε, μηδὲ μεγήρῃς
ἡμῖν εὐχομένοισι τελευτῆσαι τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
klythi, Poseidaon gaiēoche, mēde megērēis
hēmin euchomenoisi teleutēsai tade erga.
sentences.l:
“Hear, Poseidon earth-holder, and do not begrudge
us, as we pray, to accomplish these deeds.
sentences.i: “Hear, Poseidon, earth-holder, and do not begrudge us, as we pray, the accomplishing of these deeds.
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear', a regular opening word of a prayer. Ποσείδαον is the vocative, with the accent thrown back. γαιήοχος is 'earth-holder' or 'earth-carrier'; which verb lies behind -οχος is debated. μηδὲ μεγήρῃς is a prohibition with the aorist subjunctive of μεγαίρω 'grudge'. ἡμῖν εὐχομένοισι is dative, 'to us as we pray', with a dative plural in -οισι; the infinitive τελευτῆσαι 'to bring to fulfilment' gives what is not to be grudged. τάδε ἔργα 'these deeds' are the purpose of the journey, left unnamed before the Pylians.

sentences.t:
Νέστορι μὲν πρώτιστα καὶ υἱάσι κῦδος ὄπαζε,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ ἄλλοισι δίδου χαρίεσσαν ἀμοιβὴν
σύμπασιν Πυλίοισιν ἀγακλειτῆς ἑκατόμβης.
sentences.tr:
Nestori men prōtista kai huiasi kydos opaze,
autar epeit’ alloisi didou chariessan amoibēn
sympasin Pylioisin agakleitēs hekatombēs.
sentences.l:
To Nestor first of all and to his sons grant glory,
and then to the others give a gracious return,
to all the Pylians together, for the glorious hecatomb.
sentences.i: To Nestor first of all, and to his sons, grant glory, and then give the rest, all the Pylians together, a gracious return for their glorious hecatomb.
sentences.n: ὄπαζε 'grant, bestow' and δίδου 'give' are present imperatives. πρώτιστα is a double superlative, 'first of all'. κῦδος is glory, the lustre of success that a god gives. χαρίεσσαν 'gracious, pleasing' agrees with ἀμοιβήν 'return, exchange': the god is asked to repay the sacrifice with a favour, as prayer rests on gift and return. ἀγακλειτῆς ἑκατόμβης is a genitive of exchange, 'in return for the glorious hecatomb'. A ἑκατόμβη is nominally a hundred oxen; here it is the eighty-one bulls of lines 7–8. υἱάσι is the stem υἱ- seen at line 32.

sentences.t:
δὸς δ’ ἔτι Τηλέμαχον καὶ ἐμὲ πρήξαντα νέεσθαι,
οὕνεκα δεῦρ’ ἱκόμεσθα θοῇ σὺν νηὶ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.tr:
dos d’ eti Tēlemachon kai eme prēxanta neesthai,
houneka deur’ hikomestha thoēi syn nēi melainēi.
sentences.l:
And grant besides that Telemachus and I, having accomplished it, return home,
for the sake of which we came here with our swift black ship.”
sentences.i: And grant besides that Telemachus and I may return home having accomplished the thing for which we came here in our swift black ship.”
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, 'grant', with an accusative and infinitive, Τηλέμαχον καὶ ἐμὲ … νέεσθαι. πρήξαντα, aorist participle of πρήσσω (Attic πράξαντα, with Ionic η), agrees with the nearer accusative ἐμέ, though it belongs to both. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive 'return home' (Attic νεῖσθαι). οὕνεκα is here οὗ ἕνεκα in its first sense, 'for the sake of which'. ἱκόμεσθα has the epic ending -μεσθα (Attic -μεθα). θοός 'swift' and μέλαινα 'black' are both standing epithets of ships, whose hulls were tarred. The prayer ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔπειτ’ ἠρᾶτο καὶ αὐτὴ πάντα τελεύτα.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ epeit’ ērato kai autē panta teleuta.
sentences.l: So then she prayed, and herself was bringing all of it to fulfilment.
sentences.i: So she prayed, and she herself was bringing it all to pass.
sentences.n: ἠρᾶτο is the imperfect of ἀράομαι 'pray', augmented (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-). τελεύτα is an unaugmented imperfect of τελευτάω, contracted (Attic ἐτελεύτα). αὐτή, 'she herself', makes the irony plain: the goddess prays to Poseidon for a success that she is herself bringing about. The verb takes up τελευτῆσαι from line 56, so the prayer and its fulfilment are told in the same word.

sentences.t: δῶκε δὲ Τηλεμάχῳ καλὸν δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον·
sentences.tr: dōke de Tēlemachōi kalon depas amphikypellon·
sentences.l: And she gave to Telemachus the fair double cup;
sentences.i: Then she gave Telemachus the fine double cup;
sentences.n: δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist met at line 40. καλός is 'fine, fair'. The meaning of ἀμφικύπελλος is disputed. It is made from ἀμφί 'on both sides' and κύπελλον 'cup', and was explained in antiquity as a double cup, with a bowl at each end so that either could serve as the foot; others take it as 'two-handled'. It is rendered 'double' here, and the doubt is stated. The cup passes on from the elder guest to the younger, as Peisistratus asked.

sentences.t: ὣς δ’ αὔτως ἠρᾶτο Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός.
sentences.tr: hōs d’ autōs ērato Odyssēos philos huios.
sentences.l: And in just the same way prayed Odysseus' dear son.
sentences.i: And in just the same way the dear son of Odysseus prayed.
sentences.n: ὣς δ’ αὔτως is 'and in just the same way', with αὔτως 'just so'. ἠρᾶτο repeats the verb of line 62. Ὀδυσσῆος φίλος υἱός, 'Odysseus' dear son', is a line-end formula for Telemachus and takes a fixed English. Ὀδυσσῆος has the epic genitive ending -ῆος (Attic -έως). φίλος with kin serves as much for 'his own' as for 'dear'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ ὤπτησαν κρέ’ ὑπέρτερα καὶ ἐρύσαντο,
μοίρας δασσάμενοι δαίνυντ’ ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei ōptēsan kre’ hypertera kai erysanto,
moiras dassamenoi dainynt’ erikydea daita.
sentences.l:
And they, when they had roasted the outer meat and drawn it off,
having divided the portions, feasted a glorious feast.
sentences.i: And when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off the spits, they divided up the portions and feasted a glorious feast.
sentences.n: ὤπτησαν, aorist of ὀπτάω 'roast', keeps its augment (ὀ- lengthened to ὠ-). κρέ’ ὑπέρτερα, literally 'the upper meat', is the outer flesh, the meat proper, as against the σπλάγχνα tasted first. ἐρύσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω 'draw', here 'drew off the spits'. δασσάμενοι is the aorist participle of δατέομαι 'divide', with the doubled σ that epic allows. δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο, an unaugmented imperfect of δαίνυμι 'feast', with the cognate accusative δαῖτα, 'feasted a feast'. ἐρικυδής is 'very glorious', with the intensive prefix ἐρι-.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
tois ara mythōn ērche Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
among them then of speeches made-beginning the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the Gerenian horseman Nestor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: The first line is a formula for the end of a meal and keeps the English it has at 1.150. ἐξ … ἕντο is tmesis of ἐξίημι 'send out, put away', with ἔρον 'desire' as object; πόσιος and ἐδητύος depend on ἔρον, 'desire for drink and food'. τοῖς is the pronoun, 'among them', and μύθων ἦρχε is 'began the speaking'. Γερήνιος, Nestor's standing epithet, is of uncertain meaning: the ancients connected it with Gerenia or Gerenon in Messenia, where Nestor was said to have been brought up; a link with γέρων 'old man' or γέρας 'honour' has also been proposed. ἱππότα 'horseman' is a nominative in short -α, an old type found among titles.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὴ κάλλιόν ἐστι μεταλλῆσαι καὶ ἐρέσθαι
ξείνους, οἵ τινές εἰσιν, ἐπεὶ τάρπησαν ἐδωδῆς.
sentences.tr:
nyn dē kallion esti metallēsai kai eresthai
xeinous, hoi tines eisin, epei tarpēsan edōdēs.
sentences.l:
“Now indeed it is more seemly to inquire and to ask
the strangers who they are, since they have had their fill of food.
sentences.i: “Now is surely the better time to question the strangers and ask them who they are, since they have had their fill of food.
sentences.n: Nestor keeps the custom of hospitality: a guest is fed first and questioned afterwards. κάλλιον 'finer, more fitting' is the neuter comparative of καλός. μεταλλῆσαι, from μεταλλάω 'inquire', and ἐρέσθαι 'ask' are near-synonyms paired for fullness. οἵ τινες is the indirect interrogative ὅστις in the plural, 'who'. τάρπησαν is an unaugmented aorist passive of τέρπω (Attic ἐτάρπησαν), 'had their fill of', with the genitive ἐδωδῆς 'food'. These two lines are spoken partly to his own people before he turns to the guests.

sentences.t: ὦ ξεῖνοι, τίνες ἐστέ;
sentences.tr: ō xeinoi, tines este;
sentences.l: O strangers, who are you?
sentences.i: Strangers, who are you?
sentences.n: Nestor now turns to the guests themselves. ὦ with the vocative ξεῖνοι is a courteous, somewhat formal address, and ξεῖνοι, as at line 34, is both 'strangers' and 'guests'. τίνες ἐστέ asks for name and people. The questions come as a series, each closed by a question mark, and the first asks only who they are.

sentences.t: πόθεν πλεῖθ’ ὑγρὰ κέλευθα;
sentences.tr: pothen pleith’ hygra keleutha;
sentences.l: From where do you sail the watery ways?
sentences.i: From where have you come sailing over the watery ways?
sentences.n: πόθεν is 'from where?', with the suffix -θεν of place from which. πλεῖθ’ is πλεῖτε, elided, the τ roughened to θ before the rough breathing of ὑγρά. ὑγρὰ κέλευθα, 'the watery ways', is an accusative of the space travelled over: the sea is imagined as a set of paths. κέλευθα is a neuter plural beside the feminine singular κέλευθος; Homer has both. ὑγρός is simply 'wet, fluid'.

sentences.l:
Is it on some business, or at random that you wander,
as pirates do over the salt-sea, who roam about,
staking their lives, bringing evil to men of other lands?”
sentences.i: Is it on some business, or are you roaming at random, as pirates do who wander over the sea, staking their lives and bringing harm to men of other lands?”
sentences.n: ἤ … ἦ sets out the alternatives, 'is it … or …?'. κατὰ πρῆξιν is 'on business', with Ionic η (Attic πρᾶξιν). μαψιδίως is 'at random, idly'. ἀλάλησθε is a perfect of ἀλάομαι 'wander', with present sense. οἷά τε 'just as' introduces the comparison, with the epic τε that marks a general type. ὑπεὶρ is ὑπέρ lengthened for the verse. τοί is the article-form as a relative, 'who'. ἀλόωνται shows diectasis (Attic ἀλῶνται). ψυχὰς παρθέμενοι, from παρατίθημι, is 'setting their lives at stake'. The question is a plain one and not an insult: piracy was an acknowledged way of life. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα
θαρσήσας·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda
tharsēsas·
sentences.l:
To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face,
taking courage;
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face, taking courage;
sentences.n: The line is the reply-formula of line 21, here with τόν 'him', and it keeps the English it has had since Book 1. This time it runs on past its usual end into one more word, θαρσήσας, the aorist participle of θαρσέω 'take courage'. The raised point after it opens a word of explanation from the narrator before the speech begins. The courage is the point: at lines 22–24 Telemachus doubted that he could speak to Nestor at all.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ γὰρ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θάρσος Ἀθήνη
θῆχ’, ἵνα μιν περὶ πατρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο ἔροιτο
ἠδ’ ἵνα μιν κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποισιν ἔχῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
autē gar eni phresi tharsos Athēnē
thēch’, hina min peri patros apoichomenoio eroito
ēd’ hina min kleos esthlon en anthrōpoisin echēisin·
sentences.l:
for Athena herself in his mind courage
had put, so that he might ask him about his father, gone away,
and so that good fame among men may hold him:
sentences.i: for Athena herself had put courage into his heart, so that he might ask him about his father, who was gone, and so that a good name may be his among men:
sentences.n: θάρσος 'courage' takes up θαρσήσας. θῆχ’ is θῆκε, elided and aspirated before the rough breathing of ἵνα, the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι (Attic ἔθηκε). The first μιν is Nestor, who is to be asked; the second is Telemachus, whom fame is to hold. ἔροιτο is optative after the past verb, while ἔχῃσιν, a subjunctive in -ῃσι, keeps the second aim, his good name, still to come; the English keeps the shift of mood. From ἵνα on, line 77 repeats the words of 1.135 and line 78 repeats 1.95, and both take the English they have there, with 'him' for Nestor.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη, μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν,
εἴρεαι ὁππόθεν εἰμέν·
sentences.tr:
ō Nestor Nēlēïadē, mega kydos Achaiōn,
eireai hoppothen eimen·
sentences.l:
“O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
you ask from where we are;
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, you ask where we are from;
sentences.n: Νηληϊάδη is the vocative of the patronymic Νηληϊάδης 'son of Neleus', the father named at line 4. μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν, 'great glory of the Achaeans', calls the man himself the glory, the κῦδος that Athena asked Poseidon to grant him at line 57; the whole line is a formal address. εἴρεαι is the second singular of εἴρομαι 'ask', an epic by-form of ἔρομαι, with its ending left open. ὁππόθεν, with the doubled π of epic, is the indirect form of πόθεν, echoing Nestor's own question at line 71. εἰμέν is Attic ἐσμέν 'we are'.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: egō de ke toi katalexō.
sentences.l: and I will recount it to you.
sentences.i: and I will tell you all of it.
sentences.n: κε is the epic equivalent of ἄν, but Homer can join it to a future indicative or to a subjunctive, giving 'as you ask, then'. καταλέξω may be either, a future or an aorist subjunctive, since the forms are the same. τοι is the enclitic dative 'to you' (Attic σοι). καταλέγω is 'recount in order, tell in full', and it returns as the imperative κατάλεξον at line 97.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς ἐξ Ἰθάκης ὑπονηίου εἰλήλουθμεν·
sentences.tr: hēmeis ex Ithakēs hyponēiou eilēlouthmen·
sentences.l: We from Ithaca under-Neion have come;
sentences.i: We have come from Ithaca below Mount Neion;
sentences.n: ὑπονήιος is 'under Neion', formed from ὑπό and the name of a mountain, Νήιον. Which height the name belongs to, and whether it is Ithaca's own, is not certain. εἰλήλουθμεν is the epic perfect of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἐληλύθαμεν), with the lengthened reduplication εἰλ-. Telemachus names his island first; in the lines that follow he names his father, and lets that stand for his own name.

sentences.t: πρῆξις δ’ ἥδ’ ἰδίη, οὐ δήμιος, ἣν ἀγορεύω.
sentences.tr: prēxis d’ hēd’ idiē, ou dēmios, hēn agoreuō.
sentences.l: and the business is this, private, not public, which I tell of.
sentences.i: The business I speak of is a private one, not public.
sentences.n: πρῆξις answers Nestor's κατὰ πρῆξιν at line 72: yes, they come on business. ἰδίη 'private, one's own' and δήμιος 'of the people, public' set two kinds of errand apart, and he does not come as an envoy of his people. ἥδ’ is ἥδε 'this', and ἰδίη has Ionic η. ἣν ἀγορεύω is a relative clause, 'which I declare'. ἀγορεύω, the verb of the ἀγορή 'assembly', is here simply 'speak of'.

sentences.t:
πατρὸς ἐμοῦ κλέος εὐρὺ μετέρχομαι, ἤν που ἀκούσω,
δίου Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, ὅν ποτέ φασι
σὺν σοὶ μαρνάμενον Τρώων πόλιν ἐξαλαπάξαι.
sentences.tr:
patros emou kleos eury meterchomai, ēn pou akousō,
diou Odyssēos talasiphronos, hon pote phasi
syn soi marnamenon Trōōn polin exalapaxai.
sentences.l:
Of my father the wide fame I go after, if somewhere I may hear it,
heavenly Odysseus the enduring-minded, who once, they say,
fighting with you, sacked the city of the Trojans.
sentences.i: I have come after the wide fame of my father, in case I may hear of it somewhere, the fame of heavenly, steadfast Odysseus, who, they say, once fought at your side and sacked the city of the Trojans.
sentences.n: κλέος is literally 'what is heard', and here it is at once his father's fame and any report of him. μετέρχομαι is 'go after, seek'. ἤν is the epic form of ἐάν, and ἤν που ἀκούσω, 'if somewhere I may hear', echoes the words Athena used of this journey at 1.94 (ἤν που ἀκούσῃ), now in the first person. δίου Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, 'heavenly … the enduring-minded', agrees with πατρός a line earlier. μαρνάμενον, from μάρναμαι 'fight', agrees with ὅν. ἐξαλαπάξαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐξαλαπάζω 'sack utterly', depending on φασι.

sentences.t:
ἄλλους μὲν γὰρ πάντας, ὅσοι Τρωσὶν πολέμιζον,
πευθόμεθ’, ἧχι ἕκαστος ἀπώλετο λυγρῷ ὀλέθρῳ,
κείνου δ’ αὖ καὶ ὄλεθρον ἀπευθέα θῆκε Κρονίων.
sentences.tr:
allous men gar pantas, hosoi Trōsin polemizon,
peuthometh’, hēchi hekastos apōleto lygrōi olethrōi,
keinou d’ au kai olethron apeuthea thēke Kroniōn.
sentences.l:
For all the others, as many as fought with the Trojans,
we learn of, where each perished by a bitter destruction,
but of that man even the destruction the son of Cronus made unlearned.
sentences.i: For of all the others who fought against the Trojans we hear where each one perished in bitter destruction, but the son of Cronus has put even that man's destruction beyond all learning.
sentences.n: ἄλλους μέν … κείνου δ’ sets all the others against the one man. πολέμιζον is an unaugmented imperfect of πολεμίζω, with the dative Τρωσίν, 'fought with the Trojans'. πευθόμεθ’ is πευθόμεθα, from πεύθομαι, the epic by-form of πυνθάνομαι; ἄλλους is its object, 'we learn about', anticipating the ἧχι clause. ἧχι is 'where' (Attic οὗ). ἀπώλετο, from ἀπόλλυμι, keeps its augment (ὀ- lengthened to ὠ-). ἀπευθής 'unlearned, not found out' is built on the root of πεύθομαι, so the verb comes back in the adjective. θῆκε is unaugmented, and Κρονίων, 'son of Cronus', is Zeus.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις δύναται σάφα εἰπέμεν ὁππόθ’ ὄλωλεν,
εἴθ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπ’ ἠπείρου δάμη ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσιν,
εἴτε καὶ ἐν πελάγει μετὰ κύμασιν Ἀμφιτρίτης.
sentences.tr:
ou gar tis dynatai sapha eipemen hoppoth’ olōlen,
eith’ ho g’ ep’ ēpeirou damē andrasi dysmeneessin,
eite kai en pelagei meta kymasin Amphitritēs.
sentences.l:
For no one can clearly say where he has perished,
whether he on the mainland was overcome by hostile men,
or else on the open sea, among the waves of Amphitrite.
sentences.i: For no one can say for certain where he perished, whether he was brought down by hostile men on land or out on the open sea among the waves of Amphitrite.
sentences.n: εἰπέμεν is an epic aorist infinitive in -έμεν (Attic εἰπεῖν). ὁππόθ’ is ὁππόθι 'where', elided; it cannot be ὁππότε 'when', whose τ would stay unaspirated before the smooth breathing of ὄλωλεν. 'Where' also fits the choice of land or sea that follows. ὄλωλεν is the perfect of ὄλλυμι, 'has perished, is lost'. ὅ γ’ is the pronoun, 'he'. δάμη, the unaugmented aorist passive of δάμνημι 'overcome' (Attic ἐδάμη), takes a dative of the agent. δυσμενέεσσιν is a dative in -εσσι of δυσμενής 'hostile'. πέλαγος is the open sea, and Amphitrite, a sea-goddess, stands here for the sea itself.

sentences.t:
τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ’ ἱκάνομαι, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα
κείνου λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ἐνισπεῖν, εἴ που ὄπωπας
ὀφθαλμοῖσι τεοῖσιν ἢ ἄλλου μῦθον ἄκουσας
πλαζομένου·
sentences.tr:
touneka nyn ta sa gounath’ hikanomai, ai k’ ethelēistha
keinou lygron olethron enispein, ei pou opōpas
ophthalmoisi teoisin ē allou mython akousas
plazomenou·
sentences.l:
Therefore now to your knees I come, in case you may be willing
of that man the bitter destruction to tell, if somewhere you saw it
with your own eyes, or from another heard the tale,
a wanderer;
sentences.i: That is why I have come now to your knees, in the hope that you may be willing to tell me of his bitter destruction, if you perhaps saw it with your own eyes, or heard the tale from some other wanderer;
sentences.n: To come to a man's knees is the posture of a suppliant, who clasps them to ask a favour; here it is a figure for his plea. γούναθ’ is γούνατα, elided and aspirated before ἱκάνομαι. αἴ κ’ is epic εἰ with κε, 'in case, in the hope that', with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃσθα, which has the old second-person ending -σθα. τεοῖσιν is the epic form of σοῖς 'your'. ὄπωπας is a perfect of ὁράω 'see'. ἄκουσας is unaugmented (Attic ἤκουσας) and takes the genitive of the source, ἄλλου. πλαζομένου most naturally agrees with ἄλλου, 'another, a wanderer'; some take it of Odysseus, 'the tale of him wandering'.

sentences.t: πέρι γάρ μιν ὀιζυρὸν τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr: peri gar min oizyron teke mētēr.
sentences.l: for beyond all others his mother bore him to misery.
sentences.i: for his mother bore him to more misery than any other man.
sentences.n: πέρι, with the accent thrown back, is the adverb 'beyond all, exceedingly'. μιν is Odysseus. ὀιζυρόν 'wretched, full of misery' is predicative: 'bore him (to be) wretched'. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω (Attic ἔτεκε). The thought is that a man's portion of suffering is set at his birth, and his father's portion was larger than any other man's.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τί μ’ αἰδόμενος μειλίσσεο μηδ’ ἐλεαίρων,
ἀλλ’ εὖ μοι κατάλεξον ὅπως ἤντησας ὀπωπῆς.
sentences.tr:
mēde ti m’ aidomenos meilisseo mēd’ eleairōn,
all’ eu moi katalexon hopōs ēntēsas opōpēs.
sentences.l:
And do not at all, out of respect, soften things for me, nor out of pity,
but recount to me well how you came upon the sight.
sentences.i: Do not soften anything for me out of respect or pity, but tell me plainly how you came to see it.
sentences.n: μηδέ with the imperative μειλίσσεο forbids: 'do not soften (the truth)'. μειλίσσεο is the present imperative middle of μειλίσσω 'soothe, make mild', with its ending left open. αἰδόμενος 'out of respect, from delicacy' is from αἴδομαι, the verb of αἰδώς at lines 14 and 24: now Telemachus asks the old man not to let that same restraint keep back the truth. ἐλεαίρων is from ἐλεαίρω, the epic by-form of ἐλεέω 'pity'. κατάλεξον is the aorist imperative of καταλέγω. ἤντησας, augmented (ἀ- lengthened to ἠ-), is 'you met with', with the genitive ὀπωπῆς 'the sight'.

sentences.t:
λίσσομαι, εἴ ποτέ τοί τι πατὴρ ἐμός, ἐσθλὸς Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἢ ἔπος ἠέ τι ἔργον ὑποστὰς ἐξετέλεσσε
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ’ Ἀχαιοί,
τῶν νῦν μοι μνῆσαι, καί μοι νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες.
sentences.tr:
lissomai, ei pote toi ti patēr emos, esthlos Odysseus,
ē epos ēe ti ergon hypostas exetelesse
dēmōi eni Trōōn, hothi paschete pēmat’ Achaioi,
tōn nyn moi mnēsai, kai moi nēmertes enispes.
sentences.l:
I beseech you, if ever for you my father, good Odysseus,
either a word or some deed having promised, fulfilled it
in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans,
of these things now for me be mindful, and tell me the unerring truth.”
sentences.i: I beseech you, if ever my father, good Odysseus, promised you some word or deed and made it good in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes, remember it now for my sake, and tell me the unerring truth.”
sentences.n: λίσσομαι 'I beseech' is followed by the ground of the appeal, a past service, as in a prayer. ὑποστάς, aorist participle of ὑφίστημι, is 'having undertaken, promised'. ἐξετέλεσσε, aorist of ἐκτελέω with the epic doubled σ, keeps its augment (ἐξ-ε-τέλεσσε): 'carried out in full'. ἔνι is ἐν, with the accent thrown back after its noun. ὅθι is 'where'. πάσχετε is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἐπάσχετε), 'you Achaeans were suffering'. τῶν is the pronoun, a genitive with μνῆσαι, the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκω 'remember'. ἐνίσπες is an aorist imperative, 'tell'. Telemachus's speech ends here, at 3.101; Nestor's answer begins the next part.
